takeaway: 3L-Cache prunes training work, samples likely-cold objects, and auto-tunes itself to make learned cache eviction much cheaper while retaining strong miss ratios across diverse traces.
background: A cache keeps a limited subset of objects close to users. Its eviction policy decides what to discard, and operators care about both object misses, which add request latency, and byte misses, which add origin-server traffic. Per-object learned policies can predict future reuse better than simple heuristics such as LRU, but their continuous training and prediction consume substantial CPU.
villain: Existing object-level learned policies spend most of their computation on frequent model training and predictions over many eviction candidates. Random candidate sampling can also select popular objects, while fixed parameters fail to adapt to different workload traces and cache sizes.
approach: 3L-Cache trains a gradient-boosting model on filtered object histories, using a dynamically sized window and six lightweight reuse features. At eviction time it samples both old objects near the LRU tail and newly admitted objects, accumulates predictions in a heap-plus-hash-table structure, evicts half of each candidate batch, and adjusts sampling and history parameters from observed outcomes.
impact: If the reported results generalize, cache operators could obtain much of the miss-ratio benefit of per-object learning without paying the extreme CPU cost of earlier learned policies, making such policies more plausible in large cache fleets.

evaluation.overview: The authors replay 4,855 production traces from eight public datasets through a simulator, compare miss ratios and CPU cost across two cache sizes, test individual mechanisms, and compare a working prototype with simulation.
evaluation.implemented: A 3L-Cache simulator built on libCacheSim and a Python HTTP-cache prototype.
evaluation.setting: The trace study covers about 266.95 billion requests from block, object, KV, and CDN workloads, with cache sizes set to 0.1% and 10% of each trace footprint. Prototype experiments run on a dual-Xeon Dell EMC Edge T640 with 192 GB RAM.

results.text: The paper reports that 3L-Cache lowers average CPU overhead by 60.9% versus HALP and 94.9% versus LRB; its mean overhead is 6.4× LRU for small caches and 3.4× LRU for large caches.
results.locator: PDF pp. 2 and 11–12; Abstract and §5.3, Figure 10 and Table 5

results.text: Across the 4,855 traces, the authors report the lowest byte miss ratio on 69.8% of small-cache and 41.2% of large-cache cases, and the lowest object miss ratio on 66.3% and 29.3%, respectively.
On one Tencent CBS trace, the prototype's byte-hit ratio stays within 2% of simulation, while its CPU overhead is reported as 3×–6× LRU.

limitations: The paper explicitly warns that bidirectional sampling may degrade toward random sampling on atypical workloads that are less Zipf-like. Results primarily come from trace replay; the prototype check uses one Tencent CBS trace. Optimizing byte misses and object misses also requires different eviction weights, and sampling can lose to policies that score every object at larger cache sizes.
phd_group_signal: The work signals a systems style that starts with an overhead breakdown, turns the dominant costs into targeted mechanisms, and then combines broad trace replay with a smaller end-to-end prototype. It spans cache algorithms, online learning, and production-minded cost analysis without making claims about advisor quality.
beginner_concepts: object miss ratio versus byte miss ratio

claims.text: The authors implement four linked mechanisms: filtered online-training data, bidirectional candidate sampling, heap-based reuse prediction management, and workload-driven parameter tuning.
